summary: Registers the SASL mechanisms SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS, gives guidance on implementing the original SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS securely, and updates the SCRAM registration procedures in RFC 5802.

eli5.summary: This is a way to prove you know a password without sending the password, now using a stronger scrambler.

questions: what is the minimum scram iteration count
how does scram-sha-256 differ from scram-sha-1
subtitle: A short RFC that adds SHA-256 versions of the SCRAM password login and tightens the rules for using channel binding safely.

tldr.problem: The SCRAM login mechanisms in RFC 5802 were built on SHA-1, and it was later found that TLS does not have the expected properties for the tls-unique channel binding to be secure.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7677 registers SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS, defined exactly like the SHA-1 versions except that HMAC() and H() use SHA-256, and it adds a rule for using the -PLUS mechanisms safely over TLS.
tldr.outcome: SHA-256 is expected to give SCRAM greater longevity. The RFC also updates RFC 5802's registration procedures and was itself later updated by RFC 9266.

today: RFC 7677 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5802, and it has itself been updated by RFC 9266. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why a SHA-256 Version
sections.content:
RFC 7677 registers two SASL mechanisms, SCRAM-SHA-256 and SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS. SHA-256 has stronger security properties than SHA-1, and the RFC expects SCRAM mechanisms based on it to have greater predicted longevity than the SHA-1 ones.

The document does three things: it registers the two new mechanisms, it gives guidance for secure implementation of the original SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS, and it updates the SCRAM registration procedures of RFC 5802.

There was a second trigger. After RFC 5802 was published, it was discovered that Transport Layer Security (TLS) does not have the expected properties for the tls-unique channel binding to be secure. So the RFC carries normative text that applies to both the old SHA-1 PLUS mechanism and the new SHA-256 one.
sections.eli5: The old scrambler had started to look weak, so this RFC adds a stronger one. It also fixes a gap that people found in the lock-on-the-door part.

sections.title: What SCRAM-SHA-256 Changes
sections.content:
The RFC does not redefine SCRAM. The two new mechanisms are defined in the same way as SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS in RFC 5802, except that the hash function for HMAC() and H() uses SHA-256 instead of SHA-1, as specified in RFC 6234.

The -PLUS variant is the one that uses channel binding; the plain variant is for clients that do not support it.

One concrete parameter is set: the hash iteration-count announced by a server SHOULD be at least 4096. The GSS-API mechanism OID for SCRAM-SHA-256 is 1.3.6.1.5.5.18.
sections.eli5: It is the same game as before with the same rules. Only the scrambling tool inside is stronger, and the server is asked to scramble at least 4096 times.

sections.title: An Example Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC gives a simple SCRAM-SHA-256 exchange for a client that does not support channel bindings, using the username user and the password pencil.

The client opens with the username and a random nonce. The server answers with its own extended nonce, a salt (s=) and the iteration count (i=4096). The client then sends a proof (p=), and the server finishes with its own verification value (v=). The password itself never appears in the exchange.
sections.eli5: You and the server trade four short notes. Each note proves a bit more that you both know the secret, but the secret itself is never written on any of them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations from RFC 5802 still apply. On top of that:

  • To be secure, SCRAM-SHA-256-PLUS and SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS MUST be used over a TLS channel that has had the session hash extension (RFC 7627) negotiated, or session resumption MUST NOT have been used.
  • The strength of the mechanism depends in part on the hash iteration-count, written i in RFC 5802.

As a rule of thumb, the iteration count should make a modern machine take 0.1 seconds to perform the complete algorithm. The RFC notes that this is unlikely to be practical on mobile devices, that the rule gives around 15,000 iterations at the time of writing, and that 4096 iterations takes around 0.5 seconds on current mobile handsets. The cost can be avoided by caching the ClientKey, if the salt and iteration count are stable.

The recommendation is therefore that the count SHOULD be at least 4096, with careful consideration given to a significantly higher value where mobile use is less important. The RFC also points to RFC 4270 and RFC 6194 for reasons to move from SHA-1 to a strong mechanism like SHA-256.
sections.eli5: The more times the server scrambles the password, the harder it is for a thief to guess it, but the slower things get on a phone. So the RFC picks a floor of 4096 and says to go higher when you can.

sections.title: Registering the SCRAM Family
sections.content:
The IANA section updates how SCRAM mechanisms are registered. The registration for the SCRAM-* family in the SASL registry (RFC 4422) gets an updated review email address and a changed note. Members of the family MUST be explicitly registered using the "IETF Review" procedure (RFC 5226), with reviews requested on the KITTEN mailing list.

A new registry, "SASL SCRAM Family Mechanisms", adds two fields: the minimum iteration-count and an associated OID. The existing SCRAM-SHA-1 and SCRAM-SHA-1-PLUS entries moved into it with a minimum iteration-count of 4096 and the OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.14.

Both new mechanisms were added with a minimum iteration-count of 4096 and the OID 1.3.6.1.5.5.18. Only one OID needs to be assigned for a SCRAM-NAME and SCRAM-NAME-PLUS pair, and the same OID is given to both entries.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps a list of every official login method. This RFC adds a proper shelf for the SCRAM family and puts the two new ones on it with their ID numbers.
